beginner.summary: The adult brain is usually described as four big regions. Learning these four first gives you a map for everything else.

points.text: The four major regions are the cerebrum, the diencephalon, the brain stem, and the cerebellum.
The wrinkled outer layer of the cerebrum is the cerebral cortex. Its folding packs a large surface into the skull.
A deep groove, the longitudinal fissure, splits the cerebrum into left and right hemispheres.
Many control relationships are crossed: the right motor cortex moves the left side of the body.

expert.summary: Developmentally, the forebrain (prosencephalon) divides into telencephalon and diencephalon, the midbrain stays undivided, and the hindbrain (rhombencephalon) becomes the metencephalon and myelencephalon. The app's group hierarchy follows this scheme.

points.text: The cerebral hemispheres derive from the telencephalon and make up roughly 85% of brain mass.
The ventricles are remnants of the neural tube's cavity: lateral ventricles (telencephalon), third ventricle (diencephalon), fourth ventricle (rhombencephalon).

checks.q: Which list names the four major regions of the adult brain?
options: Cortex, white matter, ventricles, spinal cord
checks.explain: Frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital are lobes of the cerebrum, one of the four regions.

beginner.summary: The frontal lobe sits at the front of each hemisphere, in front of the central sulcus. It is mainly about movement, planning, and thinking.

points.text: The central sulcus separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe behind it.
Its back strip, the precentral gyrus, is the primary motor cortex.
The prefrontal cortex at the front supports functions behind personality, short-term memory, and consciousness.

expert.summary: Motor hierarchy within the frontal lobe: primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus), premotor area for movement planning, frontal eye fields, and Broca's area.

points.text: The premotor area plans movements; the frontal eye fields control eye movements and attention to visual stimuli.
Broca's area supports language production and the movements of speech, and in most people is present only on the left.

checks.q: Which groove separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe?
checks.explain: The lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe; the longitudinal fissure separates the hemispheres.

beginner.summary: The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus. Its main job is body sensation: touch, pressure, pain, and sensing where your body is.

points.text: Its main sensation is somatosensation, the general senses of the body.
The parieto-occipital sulcus, visible on the inner (medial) surface, separates it from the occipital lobe.

expert.summary: The postcentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 1, 2 and 3) is the primary somatosensory cortex; parietal regions also join the temporal lobe in higher visual processing.

points.text: More complex visual processing extends beyond the occipital lobe into the temporal and parietal lobes.

beginner.summary: The temporal lobe sits low on the side of each hemisphere, under the lateral sulcus. It handles hearing and plays a big part in memory.

points.text: The lateral sulcus separates the temporal lobe from the lobes above it.
Primary auditory cortex (Brodmann areas 41 and 42) lies in the superior temporal lobe.
Because parts of the temporal lobe belong to the limbic system, memory is a key temporal-lobe function.

expert.summary: The medial temporal lobe houses the hippocampal formation and amygdala; select those structures for detail.

checks.q: Primary auditory cortex is found in which lobe?
checks.explain: Brodmann areas 41 and 42 lie in the superior temporal lobe.

beginner.summary: The occipital lobe is at the very back of the brain and is where vision first reaches the cortex.

points.text: Brodmann areas 17 and 18 in the occipital lobe handle primary visual perception.
On the outer surface there is no obvious border between the occipital lobe and the parietal or temporal lobes.

expert.summary: Visual processing continues beyond primary visual cortex into temporal and parietal regions.

points.text: Complex visual processing involves the temporal and parietal lobes as well as the occipital lobe.

checks.q: Primary visual perception depends on Brodmann areas 17 and 18 in which lobe?
checks.explain: Areas 17 and 18 are in the occipital lobe.

beginner.summary: This ridge, just in front of the central sulcus, sends the commands that move your muscles.

points.text: The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex.
Control is crossed: the right motor cortex controls the left side of the body.

expert.summary: Upper motor neurons here instruct spinal cord neurons that drive skeletal muscle.

points.text: Cells of this region are upper motor neurons that instruct spinal cord cells to move skeletal muscles.
Movement planning upstream involves the premotor area and the basal nuclei.

connections.label: Just anterior to the central sulcus
Partner across the sulcus: postcentral gyrus

checks.q: The right precentral gyrus mainly controls movement of which side of the body?
checks.explain: Motor control is contralateral (crossed).

beginner.summary: This ridge, just behind the central sulcus, is where body sensations first reach the cortex.

points.text: The postcentral gyrus is the primary somatosensory cortex.
It processes touch, pressure, pain, itch, vibration, and the sense of body position.

expert.summary: Corresponds to Brodmann areas 1, 2 and 3.

points.text: The primary somatosensory cortex is identified as Brodmann areas 1, 2 and 3.

connections.label: Just posterior to the central sulcus
Partner across the sulcus: precentral gyrus

checks.q: Primary somatosensory cortex corresponds to which Brodmann areas?
checks.explain: 17/18 are visual and 41/42 are auditory.

beginner.summary: A thick band of white matter deep in the brain that links the left and right hemispheres.

points.text: The corpus callosum is the major pathway for communication between the two cerebral hemispheres.

expert.summary: The largest commissural white-matter structure of the cerebrum.

beginner.summary: A set of deep nuclei that help decide whether a movement happens. Their most important job is planning movement.

points.text: The basal nuclei compare cortical activity with the overall state of the nervous system to influence whether a movement takes place.
The caudate and putamen together form the striatum, the entry point for cortical input.

expert.summary: Two opposing loops through the thalamus gate cortical excitation, and dopamine from the substantia nigra tilts the balance between them.

points.text: Direct pathway: striatum to internal globus pallidus/substantia nigra pars reticulata to thalamus to cortex. It disinhibits the thalamus, allowing cortical excitation; dopamine activates it.
Indirect pathway: striatum to external globus pallidus to subthalamic nucleus to internal globus pallidus/pars reticulata. It reinforces thalamic inhibition; dopamine inhibits it.
Substantia nigra pars compacta releases dopamine into the striatum.

checks.q: Which two nuclei together form the striatum?
checks.explain: All cortical input to the basal nuclei enters through the striatum.

checks.q: What does dopamine do to the indirect pathway?
checks.explain: Dopamine activates the direct pathway and inhibits the indirect pathway, both favoring movement.

topics.title: Thalamus

beginner.summary: The brain's central relay hub: almost every sense passes through it on the way to the cortex.

points.text: All sensory information except smell passes through the thalamus before reaching the cortex.
It does more than relay; it also processes information, for example influencing which visual stimuli get attention.

expert.summary: About 60 nuclei, grouped on each side into anterior, medial and lateral groups, plus a reticular nucleus that regulates thalamic activity.

points.text: Motor, limbic and sensory pathways (except olfaction) pass through the thalamus; it divides into roughly 60 nuclei.
On each side the nuclei form lateral, medial and anterior groups; relay nuclei make up most of the thalamus.
The reticular nucleus projects back onto the thalamus rather than to cortex, and contributes to alertness and attention.
It receives the primary output of the basal nuclei.
The intralaminar and reticular nuclei are linked to arousal and pain regulation.

connections.label: Receives hippocampal output via the fornix (anterior nuclei)

clinical.text: An anatomic variant, the artery of Percheron (estimated in 4% to 12% of people), can cause infarction of both thalami when blocked.
After a thalamic stroke, numbness and tingling on the opposite side of the body can later turn into severe chronic pain (thalamic pain syndrome, Dejerine-Roussy).
Fatal familial insomnia is a hereditary prion disease in which abnormal protein deposits in the thalamus.

checks.q: Which sense does NOT pass through the thalamus on its way to the cortex?
checks.explain: Olfaction is the exception.

topics.short: Relay hub for senses and movement

beginner.summary: A small region below the thalamus that keeps the body's internal conditions stable.

points.text: It lies below and slightly in front of the thalamus.
It largely regulates homeostasis.

expert.summary: Controls the autonomic nervous system and, through the pituitary, the endocrine system; parts contribute to limbic functions.

points.text: It controls the autonomic nervous system and the endocrine system via the anterior pituitary.
Parts of the hypothalamus contribute to memory and emotion as part of the limbic system.
The lateral hypothalamus senses hunger and increases eating.
Nuclei of the periventricular zone mainly regulate the endocrine system; those of the medial and lateral zones regulate autonomic and somatic behavior.

checks.q: The hypothalamus mainly regulates…
checks.explain: It keeps internal conditions stable through autonomic and endocrine control.

beginner.summary: A curved structure deep in the temporal lobe that is essential for turning experiences into lasting memories.

points.text: The hippocampus is closely associated with consolidating memories and with decision-making.
It and the amygdala are involved in forming long-term memories and emotional responses.

expert.summary: Three zones (dentate gyrus, hippocampus proper, subiculum); Cornu Ammonis subfields CA1 to CA4; main output via the fornix.

points.text: It lies within the parahippocampal gyrus and bulges into the temporal (inferior) horn of the lateral ventricle.
Its three zones are the dentate gyrus, the hippocampus proper, and the subiculum.
The Cornu Ammonis is divided into subfields CA1, CA2, CA3 and CA4; CA3 receives input from dentate granule cells.
The fornix is its main outflow bundle, projecting toward the anterior thalamus and hypothalamus.

connections.label: Bulges into: temporal horn of lateral ventricle

clinical.text: Alzheimer's disease involves early loss of synapses in the hippocampus, and loss of CA1 pyramidal neurons; these changes may contribute to memory loss.
In medial temporal lobe epilepsy caused by hippocampal sclerosis, surgeons may remove the hippocampus (hippocampectomy).
After both hippocampi were largely removed to treat epilepsy, the patient H.M. could no longer form new memories (anterograde amnesia).

checks.q: The hippocampus is best known for its role in…
checks.explain: It is central to memory consolidation.

checks.q: What is the main output bundle of the hippocampus?
checks.explain: The fornix carries hippocampal output toward the anterior thalamus and hypothalamus.

beginner.summary: An almond-shaped cluster deep in the temporal lobe that helps process emotions, especially fear.

points.text: The amygdala is almond-shaped and lies in the temporal lobe, just beneath the uncus.
It helps regulate anxiety, aggression, fear conditioning, emotional memory, and social cognition.

expert.summary: About 13 nuclei in five functional groups; outputs reach the septal area, hypothalamus and mediodorsal thalamus.

points.text: Its roughly 13 nuclei sort into basolateral, cortical-like, central, other amygdaloid, and extended amygdala groups.
A dorsal output route (stria terminalis) reaches the septal area and hypothalamus; a ventral route (ventral amygdalofugal pathway) also reaches the mediodorsal thalamic nucleus.
Amygdala activation modulates how emotionally charged memories are acquired and consolidated.

clinical.text: Bilateral reductions of hippocampal and amygdala volume have been reported in PTSD.
Klüver-Bucy syndrome, a rare behavioral syndrome, can follow damage to both amygdalae.

checks.q: The amygdala is most associated with…
checks.explain: It processes fear, anxiety and emotional memory.

topics.title: Midbrain

beginner.summary: The top part of the brain stem, between the thalamus and the pons.

points.text: The brain stem (midbrain, pons, medulla) connects the forebrain to the spinal cord.
The midbrain coordinates maps of visual, auditory and body-sense space.

expert.summary: Roof (tectum) with the colliculi; floor (tegmentum); the cerebral aqueduct runs through its center.

points.text: The superior colliculus integrates visual, auditory and somatosensory input and orients the eyes toward a sound or touch.
The inferior colliculus is part of the auditory brain stem pathway and projects to the thalamus.
The cerebral aqueduct passes through the midbrain.

topics.short: Top of the brain stem; eye and ear reflexes

beginner.summary: The bulge in the middle of the brain stem; its name means bridge.

points.text: Seen from the front it is a thick bundle of white matter, the main connection to the cerebellum.

expert.summary: Pontine neurons relay descending forebrain input to the cerebellum.

points.text: Neurons in the pons relay descending forebrain input, including copies of motor commands, to the cerebellum.

beginner.summary: The lowest part of the brain stem, continuous with the spinal cord. It helps keep you breathing and your heart working.

points.text: Its white matter is continuous with the spinal cord.
It regulates cardiovascular and respiratory functions.

expert.summary: Contains cranial nerve nuclei and the inferior olive, which sends sensory input to the cerebellum.

points.text: It contains nuclei that process cranial nerve information, including the inferior olive.

checks.q: Which part of the brain stem regulates breathing and heart function?
checks.explain: The medulla regulates cardiovascular and respiratory functions.

beginner.summary: The 'little brain' at the back and bottom. It compares what you meant to do with what your body actually did, and corrects movement.

points.text: It is about 10 percent of the brain's mass and is folded like the cerebrum.
It compares motor commands from the cerebrum with sensory feedback to correct and coordinate movement.
Damage impairs fine movement control, posture, and motor learning.

expert.summary: Two hemispheres joined by the vermis; three lobes; three-layer cortex; deep nuclei provide the output.

points.text: Two hemispheres are joined by the vermis; the primary and posterolateral fissures divide it into anterior, posterior and flocculonodular lobes.
The cortex has three layers: molecular, Purkinje cell, and granular.
Deep nuclei, medial to lateral: fastigial, interposed (globose and emboliform), and dentate, the largest.
Superior, middle and inferior cerebellar peduncles attach it to the brain stem.
It receives motor-command copies via pontine neurons and sensory input via the inferior olive, and sends corrections to the midbrain.

Three functional zones: vestibulocerebellum (balance and eye control), spinocerebellum (vermis and paravermis: muscle tone and coordination) and cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres: planning and timing).

clinical.text: Cerebellar damage typically causes clumsy, poorly coordinated movement (ataxia) on the same side as the damage.

checks.q: The cerebellum's main job is to…
checks.explain: It compares intended movement with feedback and corrects it.

checks.q: Which is the largest deep cerebellar nucleus?
checks.explain: From medial to lateral: fastigial, interposed, dentate (largest).

beginner.summary: Fluid-filled spaces inside the brain, left over from the hollow tube the nervous system develops from.

points.text: Lateral ventricles sit in the hemispheres, the third ventricle in the diencephalon, and the fourth in the hindbrain.
The diencephalon forms the walls of the third ventricle.

expert.summary: The fourth ventricle continues into the spinal cord's central canal; the cerebral aqueduct links third and fourth ventricles through the midbrain.

points.text: The spinal cord's central canal is continuous with the fourth ventricle and filled with cerebrospinal fluid.

topics.title: Anterior thalamic nucleus
topics.short: Memory relay of the limbic system

beginner.summary: A nucleus at the front of the thalamus that helps you remember events.

points.text: Its connections with the hippocampus, mammillary bodies and fornix let the thalamus contribute to learning and memory of events (episodic memory).

expert.summary: A nucleus at the front of the thalamus that helps you remember events.

points.text: It belongs to the anterior nuclear group, one of the relay groups separated by the internal medullary lamina.
The mammillary bodies, a hub of limbic memory circuits, connect with the anterior thalamic nuclei.

checks.q: The anterior thalamic nucleus mainly supports…
checks.explain: Its limbic connections support episodic memory.

beginner.summary: A large nucleus in the middle part of the thalamus linked to emotion.

points.text: It is thought to help process emotion and coordinate attention to painful (noxious) information.

expert.summary: A large nucleus in the middle part of the thalamus linked to emotion.

beginner.summary: Part of the intralaminar nuclei, buried inside the internal medullary lamina.

points.text: Intralaminar nuclei are linked to arousal and to regulating pain.

expert.summary: Part of the intralaminar nuclei, buried inside the internal medullary lamina.

points.text: Intralaminar nuclei receive input from the basal ganglia and project to the cortex.

beginner.summary: One of the thalamus's two main motor nuclei, together with the ventral lateral nucleus.

points.text: The ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei are the thalamus's motor nuclei.

expert.summary: One of the thalamus's two main motor nuclei, together with the ventral lateral nucleus.

points.text: It is a relay nucleus of the lateral (ventral) nuclear group.

topics.title: Ventral lateral nucleus (VL)
topics.short: Relays cerebellum and basal ganglia to motor cortex

beginner.summary: A motor relay: it passes signals from movement-control centers to the motor cortex.

points.text: It receives input from the cerebellum and basal ganglia and relays motor information to the precentral (motor) cortex.

expert.summary: A motor relay: it passes signals from movement-control centers to the motor cortex.

points.text: The cerebrocerebellum's output reaches the thalamus through the dentate and interposed nuclei.

checks.q: The ventral lateral nucleus relays input from the cerebellum and basal ganglia to…
checks.explain: VL relays motor information to the precentral gyrus.

beginner.summary: Relays touch, pain and temperature from the body to the sensory cortex.

points.text: It receives spinal sensory pathways carrying temperature, pain, vibration, pressure, fine touch and body position, and relays them to the primary somatosensory cortex.

expert.summary: Relays touch, pain and temperature from the body to the sensory cortex.

checks.q: VPL relays sensation from the body to…
checks.explain: VPL projects to the postcentral gyrus.

beginner.summary: Relays sensation from the face, and taste, to the sensory cortex.

points.text: It receives the trigeminal (face) and taste pathways and relays facial sensation and taste to the primary somatosensory cortex.

expert.summary: Relays sensation from the face, and taste, to the sensory cortex.

checks.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays facial sensation and taste?
checks.explain: VPM handles the trigeminal and taste pathways; VPL handles the body.

beginner.summary: A relay nucleus near the top of the thalamus.

points.text: It is a relay nucleus of the lateral nuclear group.
Together with the anterior nucleus it makes up the upper, front region of the thalamus.

expert.summary: A relay nucleus near the top of the thalamus.

beginner.summary: A relay nucleus in the back part of the thalamus, next to the pulvinar.

points.text: It is a relay nucleus of the lateral nuclear group.

expert.summary: A relay nucleus in the back part of the thalamus, next to the pulvinar.

beginner.summary: A large nucleus at the back of the thalamus.

points.text: It makes up about 30 percent of the thalamus's volume in humans.
Its main roles involve combining information from several senses and orienting behavior.

expert.summary: A large nucleus at the back of the thalamus.

beginner.summary: The thalamus's vision relay.

points.text: It receives visual signals from the optic tract and relays them to the primary visual cortex along the calcarine sulcus.

expert.summary: The thalamus's vision relay.

checks.q: The lateral geniculate nucleus relays…
checks.explain: LGN relays optic tract input to the visual cortex.

beginner.summary: The thalamus's hearing relay.

points.text: It receives auditory input from the superior olive and inferior colliculus and relays it to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

expert.summary: The thalamus's hearing relay.

checks.q: The medial geniculate nucleus relays…
checks.explain: MGN relays auditory signals to the temporal lobe.

beginner.summary: Not a nucleus: a Y-shaped sheet of fibers inside the thalamus.

points.text: On each side it separates the lateral, medial and anterior nuclear groups.

expert.summary: Not a nucleus: a Y-shaped sheet of fibers inside the thalamus.

beginner.summary: A short fiber bundle connecting the mammillary bodies to the thalamus.

points.text: Through this tract the thalamus connects with limbic memory structures.

expert.summary: A short fiber bundle connecting the mammillary bodies to the thalamus.

clinical.text: In Korsakoff syndrome, damage to the mammillary bodies can extend into the thalamus through the mammillothalamic fasciculus.

topics.title: Caudate nucleus
topics.short: Part of the striatum (movement and learning input)

beginner.summary: A long, C-shaped nucleus that curves alongside the lateral ventricle.

points.text: It runs from the frontal lobe back and down into the temporal lobe.
With the putamen it forms the striatum, where cortical input enters the basal nuclei.

expert.summary: A long, C-shaped nucleus that curves alongside the lateral ventricle.

beginner.summary: A rounded nucleus deep in the hemisphere, lateral to the globus pallidus.

points.text: It lies mostly deep to the anterior frontal and parietal regions.
With the caudate it forms the striatum, the input stage of the basal nuclei.

expert.summary: A rounded nucleus deep in the hemisphere, lateral to the globus pallidus.

beginner.summary: The outer part of the globus pallidus.

points.text: In the indirect pathway, the striatum signals the external globus pallidus, which signals the subthalamic nucleus.

expert.summary: The outer part of the globus pallidus.

topics.title: Globus pallidus, internal segment (GPi)
topics.short: Main output of the basal nuclei

beginner.summary: The inner part of the globus pallidus, an output station of the basal nuclei.

points.text: Together with the substantia nigra pars reticulata it is an output nucleus projecting to the thalamus.

expert.summary: The inner part of the globus pallidus, an output station of the basal nuclei.

beginner.summary: A small lens-shaped nucleus below the thalamus.

points.text: In the indirect pathway it relays signals from the external to the internal globus pallidus.
It lies in the subthalamus, part of the diencephalon.

expert.summary: A small lens-shaped nucleus below the thalamus.

beginner.summary: A dark band in the midbrain that supplies dopamine to the striatum.

points.text: Its pars compacta releases dopamine into the striatum; its pars reticulata is an output nucleus.

expert.summary: A dark band in the midbrain that supplies dopamine to the striatum.

points.text: Dopamine activates the direct pathway and inhibits the indirect pathway.

beginner.summary: A small nucleus where emotion and motivation meet action.

points.text: It connects with the hypothalamus, ventral tegmental area, hippocampus and amygdala in a network that supports behaviors like food-seeking and escaping predators, described as the limbic-motor interface.

expert.summary: A small nucleus where emotion and motivation meet action.

beginner.summary: A curved band of cortex just above the corpus callosum.

points.text: It sits directly above the corpus callosum.
It contributes to emotion, learning and memory, and links behavior to motivational outcomes.

expert.summary: A curved band of cortex just above the corpus callosum.

beginner.summary: The cortex wrapped around the hippocampus on the inner temporal lobe.

points.text: It supports scene recognition and the encoding and retrieval of memories.

expert.summary: The cortex wrapped around the hippocampus on the inner temporal lobe.

topics.title: Fornix
topics.short: Main output tract of the hippocampus

beginner.summary: An arching bundle of fibers carrying signals out of the hippocampus.

points.text: It is the main output tract of the hippocampus.
Its columns end in the mammillary bodies.

expert.summary: An arching bundle of fibers carrying signals out of the hippocampus.

clinical.text: Lesions along the fornix impair recall memory.

beginner.summary: Two small round bumps on the underside of the brain, part of memory circuits.

points.text: They are important for episodic memory and connect with the amygdala, hippocampus and anterior thalamic nuclei.

expert.summary: Two small round bumps on the underside of the brain, part of memory circuits.

clinical.text: Thiamine deficiency can damage them, most notably in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

checks.q: The mammillary bodies are most important for…
checks.explain: They are a hub of limbic memory circuits.

topics.title: Vermis (spinocerebellum)
topics.short: Trunk posture, gait and eye movements

beginner.summary: The narrow midline strip joining the two cerebellar hemispheres.

points.text: As part of the spinocerebellum, it receives body sensation and coordinates movement and muscle tone of the trunk, head and proximal limbs.

expert.summary: The narrow midline strip joining the two cerebellar hemispheres.

clinical.text: Vermis lesions cause truncal or gait ataxia: unsteady posture and walking.

beginner.summary: The inner strip of each cerebellar hemisphere, next to the vermis.

points.text: Also part of the spinocerebellum, the paravermis coordinates the distal limbs.

expert.summary: The inner strip of each cerebellar hemisphere, next to the vermis.

beginner.summary: The large outer parts of the cerebellar hemispheres.

points.text: They receive input from motor and supplementary motor cortex via the pons and contribute to planning, timing and coordinating movement.

expert.summary: The large outer parts of the cerebellar hemispheres.

clinical.text: Hemisphere lesions cause limb ataxia, with dysmetria (over- or undershooting a target) and intention tremor, on the same side as the lesion.

checks.q: A lesion of the left cerebellar hemisphere usually causes limb ataxia on which side?
checks.explain: Cerebellar lesions typically cause ipsilateral deficits.

topics.title: Dentate nucleus
topics.short: Output nucleus of the lateral cerebellum

beginner.summary: One of the four pairs of deep cerebellar nuclei, inside each hemisphere.

points.text: The cerebellum has four pairs of deep nuclei, which carry most of its output.

expert.summary: One of the four pairs of deep cerebellar nuclei, inside each hemisphere.

points.text: Cerebrocerebellar output leaves through the dentate and interposed nuclei toward the red nucleus and thalamus.

beginner.summary: The other deep cerebellar nuclei, medial to the dentate.

points.text: The emboliform and globose nuclei together are called the interposed nuclei; with the fastigial and dentate nuclei they are the main output route of the cerebellum.

expert.summary: The other deep cerebellar nuclei, medial to the dentate.

points.text: The fastigial nuclei are linked to saccadic and vergence eye movements.

beginner.summary: The front region of the hypothalamus, above the optic chiasm.

points.text: It contains the preoptic, paraventricular, supraoptic, suprachiasmatic and anterior hypothalamic nuclei.
The suprachiasmatic nucleus receives input from the retina and synchronizes body functions with light and dark (the circadian rhythm).
The supraoptic nucleus mainly produces vasopressin; the anterior hypothalamic nucleus helps cool the body.

expert.summary: The front region of the hypothalamus, above the optic chiasm.

checks.q: Which hypothalamic nucleus sets the body's daily rhythm from light input?
checks.explain: It receives direct retinal input.

beginner.summary: The middle region of the hypothalamus, above the pituitary stalk.

points.text: It contains the arcuate, ventromedial and dorsomedial nuclei.
The dorsomedial nucleus is involved with blood pressure, heart rate and gastrointestinal stimulation.

expert.summary: The middle region of the hypothalamus, above the pituitary stalk.

topics.title: Posterior hypothalamus
topics.short: Heat conservation and arousal of the body

beginner.summary: The back region of the hypothalamus, above the mammillary bodies.

points.text: The posterior hypothalamic nucleus helps regulate blood pressure, pupil dilation and heat conservation, such as shivering in the cold.

expert.summary: The back region of the hypothalamus, above the mammillary bodies.

points.text: The posterior region also contains the mammillary nucleus, part of the limbic system.

beginner.summary: The top-most horizontal ridge of the frontal lobe.

points.text: On the dominant (usually left) side it is a key part of the network for working memory and spatial processing.
On the non-dominant side it is involved in impulse control.

expert.summary: The top-most horizontal ridge of the frontal lobe.

beginner.summary: The middle horizontal ridge of the frontal lobe.

points.text: The dominant (left) middle frontal gyrus plays a key role in literacy; the non-dominant (right) one in numeracy.
Its back part contains the frontal eye fields (Brodmann area 8), which control fast scanning eye movements (saccades).

expert.summary: The middle horizontal ridge of the frontal lobe.

beginner.summary: The lowest ridge of the frontal lobe; on the left it contains Broca's area.

points.text: The back part of the dominant (usually left) inferior frontal gyrus contains Broca's area (Brodmann areas 44 and 45), responsible for speech production.

expert.summary: The lowest ridge of the frontal lobe; on the left it contains Broca's area.

checks.q: Broca's area, important for producing speech, is in which gyrus?
checks.explain: It lies in the caudal part of the dominant inferior frontal gyrus.

beginner.summary: The very front tip of the frontal lobe, part of the prefrontal cortex.

points.text: The prefrontal cortex is a higher-order association center for decision making and personality.

expert.summary: The very front tip of the frontal lobe, part of the prefrontal cortex.

beginner.summary: The upper part of the parietal lobe behind the postcentral gyrus.

points.text: It contains somatosensory association cortex (Brodmann areas 5 and 7) involved in higher functions such as planning actions.

expert.summary: The upper part of the parietal lobe behind the postcentral gyrus.

beginner.summary: The lower part of the parietal lobe, including the supramarginal and angular gyri.

points.text: It includes the supramarginal gyrus (Brodmann area 40) and angular gyrus (area 39), and contains the secondary somatosensory cortex, which integrates input from the thalamus.

expert.summary: The lower part of the parietal lobe, including the supramarginal and angular gyri.

beginner.summary: The top ridge of the temporal lobe, just below the lateral sulcus.

points.text: It supports phonological representation, the sound structure of heard words; Wernicke's area lies in the dominant superior temporal gyrus.

expert.summary: The top ridge of the temporal lobe, just below the lateral sulcus.

beginner.summary: The middle ridge of the temporal lobe.

points.text: Part of it belongs to a semantic control network that assigns meaning to words and sounds.

expert.summary: The middle ridge of the temporal lobe.

beginner.summary: The lowest ridge on the side of the temporal lobe.

points.text: It contributes to visual and face perception as part of the ventral visual pathway, which carries information from primary visual cortex to identify what is seen.

expert.summary: The lowest ridge on the side of the temporal lobe.

beginner.summary: A bump on the back of the midbrain.

points.text: It integrates visual, auditory and body-sense information and orients the eyes toward a sound or touch.

expert.summary: A bump on the back of the midbrain.

beginner.summary: A bump on the back of the midbrain, below the superior colliculus.

points.text: It is part of the auditory pathway and projects to the thalamus, which relays sound to the cerebrum.

expert.summary: A bump on the back of the midbrain, below the superior colliculus.

beginner.summary: Lobules I to V form the front part of the cerebellum, which is mainly about movement.

points.text: Lobules I to V together make up the cerebellum's anterior lobe.
Body parts are mapped in order: toes toward the front, fingers mid-lobe, tongue near the primary fissure.
A key motor area of the cerebellar cortex sits in the middle (medial) part of this lobe.

expert.summary: The anterior lobe, with lobule VIII, holds the sensorimotor cerebellum.

points.text: Authors place the sensorimotor cerebellum in the anterior lobe and lobule VIII.
The anterior-lobe vermis is built into the hemispheres, not truly separate from them.

clinical.text: Damage here can contribute to motor problems such as ataxia, dysmetria and dysarthria, when it involves the anterior lobe and part of lobule VI.

checks.q: Which lobules make up the cerebellar anterior lobe?
checks.explain: The primary fissure separates the anterior lobe (I-V) from the posterior lobe (VI-IX).

beginner.summary: Lobule VI is the first lobule behind the primary fissure and links movement with thinking tasks.

points.text: Lobule VI belongs to the posterior lobe, which is made of lobules VI to IX.
Working-memory and executive tasks engage lobule VI, Crus I and lobule VIIB.
Lesions of lobule VI change eyeblink conditioning, a simple learned response.

expert.summary: Lobule VI shares a white matter stem with VIIA and VIIB and is counted in the cognitive cerebellum.

points.text: Lobules VI, VIIA and VIIB share a dorsally directed white matter stem; they are the only lobules to do so in the vermis.
Lobules VI and VII are described as the cognitive cerebellum.

clinical.text: Damage here can cause dysarthria, and lesions across lobules IV to VI can cause upper-limb ataxia.

checks.q: Which pair is described as the 'cognitive cerebellum' in the posterior lobe?
checks.explain: Stoodley and Schmahmann describe lobules VI and VII of the posterior lobe as the cognitive cerebellum.

beginner.summary: Crus I and Crus II are large outer lobules of the cerebellum that link to thinking areas of the cortex.

points.text: Crus I and Crus II make up most of the outer rear edge of each cerebellar hemisphere.
They connect with association cortex, including prefrontal, posterior parietal and temporal areas.
In right-handed people, language tasks activate the right rear-side cerebellum; spatial tasks tend to favor the left.

expert.summary: Crus I and II have distinctive white matter signs on imaging and a cognitive profile.

points.text: Crus I sits between two fissures (the 'bowtie sign'); the white matter stems of both crura join medially (the 'horseshoe sign').
Eyeblink conditioning maps to Crus I.

clinical.text: Damage to the posterior lobe, but not the anterior lobe, can cause cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome (executive, spatial, language and emotional changes).

checks.q: Which cortical regions do Crus I and II connect with?
checks.explain: Crus I/II and lobule VII link to prefrontal, posterior parietal and temporal association cortex.

beginner.summary: Lobule VIIB is a smaller outer lobule beside the crura, involved in thinking tasks.

points.text: Lobule VIIB adds a smaller share to the outer rear edge of the hemispheres than the crura do.
Working-memory and executive tasks engage lobule VIIB, along with lobule VI and Crus I.
The fissures separating lobules VI, VIIA and VIIB are the last to form.

expert.summary: VIIB is part of the VI-VIIA-VIIB group with a shared white matter stem.

points.text: Lobules VI, VIIA and VIIB share one dorsally directed white matter stem in the vermis.
Lobules VI and VII are described as the cognitive cerebellum.

checks.q: Which tasks engage lobule VIIB, along with VI and Crus I?
checks.explain: Stoodley and Schmahmann note working-memory and executive tasks engage these lobules.

beginner.summary: Lobule VIII is a lower cerebellar lobule that adds to movement control.

points.text: Lobule VIII helps with motor function; movement activity shows up in the anterior lobe and in lobule VIII.
Body-movement areas of the cortex show connectivity to the anterior lobe and lobule VIII.
Together with the anterior lobe, it is thought to hold the cerebellum's sensorimotor map.

expert.summary: VIIIA and VIIIB each have their own white matter stem.

points.text: VIIIA and VIIIB have separate white matter stems on T2 imaging.
The anterior lobe and lobule VIII contain the sensorimotor cerebellum.

checks.q: Lobule VIII is best linked with which function?
checks.explain: Lehman et al. report motor activity in the anterior lobe, ventral cerebellum (especially VIII) and deep nuclei.

beginner.summary: Lobule IX is a lower cerebellar lobule that helps with eye-guided movement.

points.text: The tonsils, lobule IX, extend downward and toward the middle.
Lobule IX is considered essential for movement guided by vision.
Connectivity data suggest it contributes to the default mode network, though its cognitive role is unclear.

expert.summary: Lobule IX has a marked white matter stem and a possible small additional body map.

points.text: An 'anterior diamond' of white matter marks the stem to lobule IX.
There is evidence of a small tertiary body map near lobule IX.

checks.q: Lobule IX is considered essential for which kind of movement?
checks.explain: Stoodley and Schmahmann consider lobule IX essential for visually guided movement.

beginner.summary: Lobule X is the small bottom part of the cerebellum tied to balance.

points.text: Lobule X is the flocculonodular lobe, separated from the posterior lobe by the posterolateral fissure.
It is long thought to be the vestibulocerebellum, working with the balance system.
Its nodulus presses on the fourth ventricle, and the flocculus can be seen from below.

expert.summary: Lobule X remains an essential node of the vestibular system.

points.text: Lobule X is regarded as an essential node in the vestibular system.
The cerebellum receives balance information from the vestibular nuclei.

checks.q: Lobule X is traditionally called the...
checks.explain: Lobule X has long been considered the vestibulocerebellum.

topics.title: Cerebellar white matter and deep nuclei

beginner.summary: Under the cerebellar cortex lies white matter that carries signals and holds deep nuclei.

points.text: The white matter beneath the cortex is called the arbor vitae, Latin for 'tree of life'.
Three pairs of deep nuclei sit inside it: fastigial, interposed and dentate.
Each cerebellar hemisphere controls the same side of the body.

expert.summary: Deep nuclei and peduncles route cerebellar input and output.

points.text: From medial to lateral the nuclei are fastigial, interposed (globose and emboliform), then dentate, the largest.
The superior peduncle carries fibers from dentate, emboliform and globose; the inferior from fastigial; the middle connects the cerebral cortex with the cerebellum.

clinical.text: Cerebellar dysfunction can cause ataxia, intention tremor, nystagmus and dysarthria.

checks.q: What is the cerebellar white matter called?
checks.explain: The cerebellar white matter is called the arbor vitae, 'tree of life'.

topics.title: Pituitary gland: front lobe, back lobe and stalk

beginner.summary: The pituitary is a small gland under the brain with a front lobe, a back lobe and a stalk.

points.text: The pituitary sits in a bony hollow of the sphenoid bone called the sella turcica.
The front lobe (adenohypophysis) and back lobe (neurohypophysis) do different jobs.
The stalk, called the infundibulum, links the gland to the hypothalamus.

expert.summary: Hypothalamic signals reach the anterior lobe through a portal system, while posterior hormones travel down axons.

points.text: Anterior lobe hormones include ACTH, prolactin, LH, FSH, growth hormone and TSH.
Oxytocin and vasopressin come from neurons in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei and are stored in the posterior lobe.
The infundibulum arises from the tuber cinereum and median eminence of the hypothalamus.

checks.q: Which part of the pituitary stores oxytocin and vasopressin?
checks.explain: The back lobe stores hormones made in hypothalamic neurons.

beginner.summary: The red nucleus is a midbrain structure that helps link the cerebellum with movement pathways.

points.text: It lies in the ventral midbrain.
In humans it has a larger front part (parvocellular) and a smaller back part (magnocellular).
In humans the front part makes up most of the nucleus.

expert.summary: The magnocellular part gives rise to the rubrospinal tract; the parvocellular part projects to the ipsilateral inferior olive.

points.text: The magnocellular part receives input from the opposite interposed cerebellar nuclei and gives rise to the rubrospinal tract.
The parvocellular part sends output to the same-side inferior olivary nucleus.

clinical.text: Damage here can involve nearby oculomotor fibers and contribute to Benedikt syndrome, with third nerve palsy on one side and ataxia with tremor on the other.

checks.q: Where is the red nucleus?
checks.explain: The source places it in the ventral midbrain.

beginner.summary: The brachia are fiber bundles that link the colliculi to the thalamus.

points.text: The superior brachium links each superior colliculus to the lateral geniculate body and optic tract.
The inferior brachium links each inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate nucleus.
The superior colliculus is involved in visual reflexes such as saccadic eye movements.

expert.summary: The inferior colliculus main output runs through its brachium to excite the medial geniculate nucleus.

points.text: The inferior colliculus main output runs in its brachium to excite the thalamic medial geniculate nucleus.
The inferior colliculus relays sound information from the inner ear toward auditory cortex.

checks.q: Which structure does the inferior brachium connect to?
checks.explain: The inferior brachium links the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate nucleus.

beginner.summary: Visual signals leave each eye in the optic nerve, partly cross at the chiasm, and continue in the optic tracts.

points.text: The optic nerve is cranial nerve II and carries axons of retinal ganglion cells.
The optic chiasm lies above the pituitary gland and below the hypothalamus.
At the chiasm, nasal retinal fibers cross while temporal fibers stay on the same side.

expert.summary: Each optic tract carries the contralateral visual field from both eyes, mostly to the lateral geniculate nucleus.

points.text: The optic nerve has four segments: intraocular, intraorbital, intracanalicular and intracranial.
The optic tract begins behind the chiasm; collateral fibers go to the superior colliculus, pretectal nuclei and suprachiasmatic nucleus.

clinical.text: Damage here can cause vision loss: optic nerve lesions affect one eye, pressure below the chiasm often causes bitemporal hemianopia, and tract lesions cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia.

checks.q: Which retinal fibers cross at the optic chiasm?
checks.explain: Nasal retinal fibers cross; temporal fibers stay on the same side.

beginner.summary: The insula is a hidden fold of cortex deep in the lateral sulcus.

points.text: The insula forms the floor of the lateral sulcus, covered by parts of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes.
It is involved in taste, pain, autonomic control, and risk-reward behavior.
The limen insulae is at its front-lower tip, where the middle cerebral artery generally divides.

expert.summary: The insula connects with neocortex, limbic structures and basal ganglia, with anterior and posterior regions serving different roles.

points.text: It connects with frontal, parietal and temporal cortex, olfactory bulb, anterior cingulate, amygdala, hippocampus, thalamus and basal ganglia.
fMRI shows three functional subdivisions; anterior regions relate to emotional integration and posterior regions to cognition.

clinical.text: Damage here can cause paresis, speech deficits or dizziness in rare insular-only strokes.

checks.q: Why is the insula not visible from the brain surface?
options: It is covered by the operculum
checks.explain: Frontal, parietal and temporal lobes cover it.

beginner.summary: The claustrum is a thin sheet of gray matter whose function is still debated.

points.text: It is classically described as lying between the striatum and the insular cortex.
It is a long, band-like sheet that follows the shape of the insula.
Ideas about its job include multisensory integration and filtering important signals; the evidence is limited and mixed.

expert.summary: It is reciprocally connected with cortex and has no layered organization.

points.text: About 85% of its neurons are excitatory projection cells and about 15% are interneurons.
It receives cortical input mainly from layer VI and projects most densely to layers IV and VI.

checks.q: What is the claustrum's shape?
checks.explain: The review describes a long band-like sheet.

beginner.summary: The anterior commissure is a small bundle of fibers connecting the two hemispheres.

points.text: It crosses the midline below and behind the rostrum of the corpus callosum.
It links the two hemispheres and parts of the limbic system on both sides.
It has about 3.5 million fibers, compared with about 200 million in the corpus callosum.

expert.summary: It may act as a backup for the corpus callosum.

points.text: Its posterior limb reaches temporal cortex, amygdala and temporal pole; its anterior limb links to the olfactory bulbs.
In some cases of callosal agenesis it is enlarged and may partly substitute for interhemispheric transfer.

checks.q: What does the anterior commissure connect?
checks.explain: It links the two cerebral hemispheres across the midline.

beginner.summary: A groove on the inner face of the occipital lobe that holds the brain's first visual cortex.

points.text: It lies on the inner (medial) surface and runs from the parieto-occipital sulcus back to the occipital pole.
Its upper and lower banks contain the primary visual cortex.
It splits the inner surface into the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below.

expert.summary: The calcarine sulcus houses V1 (Brodmann area 17) and separates the cuneus from the lingual gyrus.

points.text: V1 (Brodmann area 17) receives visual input from the retina by way of the thalamus.
The calcarine artery supplies the sulcus and most of the cuneus.

checks.q: Which cortex sits in the banks of the calcarine sulcus?
checks.explain: The upper and lower banks of the calcarine sulcus contain the primary visual cortex.

beginner.summary: The cuneus is the gyrus on the inner surface of the occipital lobe, just above the calcarine sulcus.

points.text: It is the upper gyrus on the inner surface of the occipital lobe, bounded by the calcarine sulcus.
The occipital lobe, which contains it, mainly handles visual processing.

expert.summary: The cuneus is the superior medial occipital gyrus, supplied mostly by the calcarine artery.

points.text: The calcarine artery supplies most of the cuneus, and the parieto-occipital artery supplies part of it.

checks.q: Where is the cuneus relative to the calcarine sulcus?
options: In front of the central sulcus
checks.explain: The cuneus is the superior medial gyrus, bounded by the calcarine sulcus.

beginner.summary: The lingual gyrus is the lower gyrus on the inner surface of the occipital lobe, below the calcarine sulcus.

points.text: It sits below the calcarine sulcus on the inner surface of the occipital lobe.
The fusiform gyrus lies below it and stretches in from the temporal lobe.

expert.summary: The lingual gyrus is the inferior medial occipital gyrus with its own artery.

points.text: The lingual gyrus artery and the posterior-temporal artery supply it.

checks.q: Which gyrus lies directly below the lingual gyrus?
checks.explain: The fusiform gyrus lies below the lingual gyrus and extends from the temporal lobe.

beginner.summary: This groove marks the border between the occipital and parietal lobes on the inner surface.

points.text: On the inner surface, it separates the occipital lobe from the parietal lobe.
The calcarine sulcus starts from it and runs back toward the occipital pole.

expert.summary: It is the medial occipito-parietal boundary and has a landmark role on the lateral surface too.

points.text: On the outer surface, the occipital border is an imaginary line from this sulcus to the preoccipital notch.
The parieto-occipital artery supplies the sulcus.

checks.q: Which two lobes does the parieto-occipital sulcus separate on the inner surface?
checks.explain: On the medial surface it separates the occipital lobe from the parietal lobe.

beginner.summary: The fusiform gyrus is on the underside of the temporal lobe and is linked to recognising what we see.

points.text: It is linked to reading, recognising objects and recognising faces.
It extends from the temporal lobe and lies below the lingual gyrus.

expert.summary: Beyond recognition, the anterior fusiform region may help hold information in working memory.

points.text: Area TF lies on the occipitotemporal sulcus and anterior fusiform gyrus; studies suggest it supports keeping information in working memory.

checks.q: Which ability is linked to the fusiform gyrus?
checks.explain: The fusiform gyrus is linked to reading, object recognition and face recognition.

beginner.summary: A groove in the temporal lobe that supports speech, faces, motion and understanding other people.

points.text: It is involved in motion, speech and face processing, and understanding language.
It also helps combine sight and sound, and is involved in theory of mind (thinking about what others think).

expert.summary: The sulcus has four functionally distinct parts with different cortical and white matter connections.

points.text: It has four parts (dorsal and ventral, anterior and posterior), each linked to different regions across the four lobes.
Its white matter links include the arcuate/superior longitudinal fasciculus, occipitotemporal U fibres and the middle longitudinal fasciculus.

checks.q: Which of these is the superior temporal sulcus involved in?
checks.explain: The sulcus is involved in motion, speech and face processing, language comprehension, audiovisual integration and theory of mind.

beginner.summary: The temporal pole is the front tip of the temporal lobe and supports language and social and emotional processing.

points.text: It supports language, reading social cues, emotional processing and recognising faces.
It also supports theory of mind, which is thinking about what other people believe or feel.

expert.summary: It has dorsal (TGd) and ventral (TGv) parts that are functionally connected but respond differently to motor tasks.

points.text: TGd (dorsal) and TGv (ventral) temporal gyrus areas are connected to each other; TGd deactivates during motor tasks while TGv activates.
The temporopolar artery, a branch of the middle cerebral artery, supplies it.

clinical.text: Damage here can affect meaning and word skills, social and emotional behaviour, face recognition, and control of eating and sexual behaviour.

checks.q: Which artery supplies the temporal pole?
checks.explain: The temporopolar artery, a branch of the middle cerebral artery, supplies the temporal pole.

beginner.summary: This gyrus is the auditory region where the hearing pathway ends in the cortex.

points.text: It is the last cortical stop of the ascending hearing pathway, where sound is perceived.
It receives input from both sides of the brain.

expert.summary: The auditory cortex is organised by sound frequency and is tuned by higher-order regions.

points.text: The auditory pathway is tonotopically organised: each auditory nucleus is arranged by sound frequency.
Prefrontal and limbic regions send signals back that adjust processing by attention and how relevant the sound is.

clinical.text: Tinnitus is linked to overactivity in one frequency-specific region of the auditory cortex.

checks.q: What does the transverse temporal gyrus mainly do?
options: It is the auditory region of the cortex
It separates the two lateral ventricles
checks.explain: The page describes it as the auditory region, the final cortical stop of the hearing pathway.

beginner.summary: These two grooves divide the side of the frontal lobe into three horizontal gyri.

points.text: Together they divide the outer frontal surface into the superior, middle and inferior frontal gyri.
The superior frontal sulcus separates the superior frontal gyrus from the middle frontal gyrus below it.
The inferior frontal sulcus separates the middle frontal gyrus from the inferior frontal gyrus, the lowest one.

expert.summary: Both sulci run forward and downward from the precentral sulcus.

points.text: The superior and inferior frontal sulci extend forward and downward from the precentral sulcus.

checks.q: Which gyrus lies between the superior and inferior frontal sulci?
checks.explain: The superior sulcus lies above the middle frontal gyrus and the inferior sulcus lies below it.

beginner.summary: A groove in the frontal lobe that runs just in front of the precentral gyrus.

points.text: It runs parallel to the central sulcus, just in front of the precentral gyrus.
The precentral gyrus, behind it, contains the primary motor cortex.

expert.summary: The precentral sulcus is the starting point of the superior and inferior frontal sulci.

points.text: The superior and inferior frontal sulci run forward and downward from it.

checks.q: Where does the precentral sulcus run?
options: Parallel to the central sulcus, in front of the precentral gyrus
Along the floor of the calcarine region
checks.explain: It runs parallel to the central sulcus, just rostral to the precentral gyrus.

beginner.summary: The central sulcus is the groove that divides the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe.

points.text: It separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe.
The precentral gyrus in front of it holds the primary motor cortex.
The postcentral gyrus behind it holds the primary somatosensory cortex.

expert.summary: It sits between the primary motor cortex (frontal) and primary somatosensory cortex (parietal).

points.text: The postcentral gyrus receives sensory information from the opposite (contralateral) side of the body.

checks.q: Which two lobes does the central sulcus separate?
checks.explain: The central sulcus separates the frontal and parietal lobes.

beginner.summary: The cingulate sulcus is a groove on the inner surface that sits above the cingulate gyrus.

points.text: It separates the cingulate gyrus from the superior frontal gyrus above it.
The cingulate gyrus wraps around the corpus callosum like a belt.
Cingulate motor areas lie within the sulcus and turn internal and external signals into motor commands.

expert.summary: The cingulate cortex includes the gyrus plus cortex lining the sulcus, and has four regions.

points.text: Cingulate cortex = the gyrus plus the grey matter lining the upper and lower borders of the cingulate sulcus.
Its four regions are anterior, midcingulate, posterior and retrosplenial cortex.

checks.q: What does the cingulate sulcus separate the cingulate gyrus from?
checks.explain: The gyrus is separated from the superior frontal gyrus above by the cingulate sulcus.

beginner.summary: Part of this lobule controls movement of the lower limb.

points.text: The medial (inner) part of the paracentral lobule contains motor control for the foot, leg and thigh.

expert.summary: The medial paracentral lobule carries lower-limb motor control.

points.text: Its medial part contains the motor representation of the foot, leg and thigh.

checks.q: Which body part's movement is controlled by the medial paracentral lobule?
checks.explain: The medial part of the paracentral lobule contains motor control of the foot, leg and thigh.

beginner.summary: The lateral ventricles are the two C-shaped fluid-filled spaces, one in each hemisphere.

points.text: Each is a C-shaped cavity inside a cerebral hemisphere, lined by ependyma, holding about 7 to 10 ml.
They are the largest of the ventricular spaces.
Each connects to the third ventricle through the interventricular foramen.

expert.summary: Each lateral ventricle has a body and three horns, spread across four lobes.

points.text: The body lies in the parietal lobe, from the interventricular foramen to the splenium of the corpus callosum.
The anterior horn is in the frontal lobe, the posterior in the occipital lobe and the inferior in the temporal lobe.
The ventral surface is usually defined by the basal ganglia and the dorsal surface by the corpus callosum.

checks.q: What shape is each lateral ventricle?
checks.explain: Each lateral ventricle is a C-shaped cavity within a cerebral hemisphere.

topics.title: Temporal horn of the lateral ventricle

beginner.summary: The temporal horn is the part of the lateral ventricle that reaches into the temporal lobe.

points.text: It is the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, lying in the temporal lobe.
It is the largest and longest of the lateral ventricle's three horns.

expert.summary: The inferior (temporal) horn is one of three horns of the C-shaped lateral ventricle.

points.text: The other horns are the anterior (frontal) horn and the posterior (occipital) horn.

checks.q: In which lobe does the temporal horn lie?
checks.explain: The inferior (temporal) horn lies in the temporal lobe.

beginner.summary: The aqueduct is a narrow channel that lets fluid pass from the third to the fourth ventricle.

points.text: It links the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle.
It runs through the midbrain.
It is the narrowest part of the ventricular system.

expert.summary: Also called the Sylvian aqueduct, it is a middle step in the CSF route and a common blockage site.

points.text: It is about 18 mm long and is the most common site of obstruction in the ventricular system.
CSF flows from the lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramina and third ventricle, then the aqueduct, into the fourth ventricle.

clinical.text: Narrowing (stenosis) of the aqueduct is a frequent cause of obstructive hydrocephalus, enlarging both lateral ventricles and the third ventricle.

checks.q: Which two ventricles does the cerebral aqueduct connect?
checks.explain: The aqueduct links the third and fourth ventricles.

beginner.summary: A thin sheet that divides the two lateral ventricles.

points.text: It is a thin vertical sheet of nervous tissue separating the two lateral ventricles.
It forms the inner (medial) wall of each lateral ventricle.

expert.summary: Ependyma covers both faces of the septum pellucidum.

points.text: Ependyma lines both surfaces of the septum, which is part of the midline sagittal surface of the hemispheres.

checks.q: What does the septum pellucidum separate?
checks.explain: It is a thin vertical sheet that separates the two lateral ventricles.

beginner.summary: This small muscle lifts your upper eyelid.

points.text: Its main job is raising the eyelid.
It does not touch the eyeball directly.
It is supplied by the upper division of the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III).

expert.summary: Levator palpebrae superioris elevates the lid and is supplied by the superior division of CN III.

points.text: It arises from the lesser wing of the sphenoid and attaches to the eyelid through its aponeurosis and the superior tarsal muscle.

checks.q: What is the main job of the levator palpebrae superioris?
checks.explain: The source says it is mainly responsible for lifting the eyelid.

beginner.summary: Four straight muscles on each eye help point your gaze in different directions.

points.text: The rectus and oblique muscles work together to move the eye into different gaze positions.
Three of the four rectus muscles are supplied by the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III).
The lateral rectus is the exception. It is supplied by the abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI).

expert.summary: All four recti arise at the annulus of Zinn; the superior rectus uses the upper division of CN III and the inferior and medial use the lower.

points.text: Each rectus starts at the annulus of Zinn and inserts on the eyeball about 5.5 to 7.7 mm from the limbus.
Superior rectus uses the upper division of CN III. Inferior and medial rectus use the lower division.

clinical.text: Weakness, injury or paralysis of the inferior rectus can cause strabismus.

checks.q: Which nerve supplies the lateral rectus?
checks.explain: The lateral rectus is supplied by cranial nerve VI, the abducens nerve.

beginner.summary: This eye muscle loops through a small pulley and helps move the eye.

points.text: It is one of the oblique muscles that help the eye reach different gaze positions.
It is supplied by the trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV).

expert.summary: Superior oblique passes through the trochlea and is the muscle supplied by CN IV.

points.text: It starts medial to the optic foramen, passes through the trochlea, and inserts just behind the superior rectus insertion.

checks.q: Which cranial nerve supplies the superior oblique?
checks.explain: The superior oblique is supplied by the trochlear nerve.

beginner.summary: The eyeball is a small sphere with three layers that catches light and sends the image to the brain.

points.text: An adult eyeball is about 2.5 cm across, and only about one-sixth of it is exposed.
Its wall has three layers: the outer fibrous layer, the middle vascular layer, and the inner retina.
The retina holds rods for dim light and cones for color vision.

expert.summary: The globe has fibrous (cornea, sclera), vascular (uvea) and neural (retina) tunics, with the fovea giving sharpest vision.

points.text: The vascular tunic includes the choroid, ciliary body and iris; the lens is held by zonular fibers from the ciliary muscles.
The fovea centralis has only cones and gives the sharpest vision. The optic disc has no photoreceptors and is the blind spot.
Aqueous humor is made by the ciliary body and drains through Schlemm's canal.

clinical.text: Damage here can include retinal detachment, where fluid collects between retinal layers and distorts vision.

checks.q: Which part of the retina gives the sharpest vision?
checks.explain: The fovea centralis has only cones and gives the sharpest vision.

beginner.summary: The masseter is a strong cheek muscle that closes your jaw when you chew.

points.text: It is a powerful muscle that lifts the jaw to close the mouth.
It also helps push the lower jaw forward.
Its motor nerve is the masseteric nerve, from the trigeminal nerve.

expert.summary: Masseter has superficial and deep heads from the zygomatic arch to the mandibular ramus and angle, supplied by V3.

points.text: The superficial head arises from the zygomatic bone and the front of the zygomatic arch; the deep head from the whole arch.
Its blood supply is mainly the masseteric artery, a branch of the maxillary artery.

clinical.text: Damage here can show up as trismus: in tetanus, rigid masseter and temporalis muscles cause it.

checks.q: What is the masseter's main action?
checks.explain: It is a powerful elevator that closes the jaw.

beginner.summary: The temporalis is a fan-shaped muscle on the side of the head that helps chew.

points.text: Its front and middle fibers lift the jaw.
Its back fibers pull the jaw backward.
It is supplied by deep temporal branches of the mandibular nerve (V3).

expert.summary: Temporalis runs from the temporal fossa to the coronoid process and elevates and retracts the mandible.

points.text: It arises from the temporal fossa and inferior temporal line and inserts on the coronoid process of the mandible.

checks.q: Where does the temporalis attach on the mandible?
checks.explain: It inserts on the coronoid process of the mandible.

beginner.summary: The medial pterygoid sits inside the jaw and helps lift and move it.

points.text: It helps raise and push forward the lower jaw.
Working with the lateral pterygoid, it helps move the jaw side to side.
Its nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve.

expert.summary: Medial pterygoid has superficial and deep heads and inserts on the medial mandibular ramus.

points.text: The superficial head arises from the maxillary tuberosity; the deep head from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate.

checks.q: Which nerve division supplies the medial pterygoid?
checks.explain: The medial pterygoid nerve is a division of the mandibular nerve.

beginner.summary: The lateral pterygoid helps open the jaw and slide it forward or side to side.

points.text: It helps lower the jaw, though the source says gravity does much of this.
It also helps push the jaw forward and move it side to side.
It is supplied by lateral pterygoid nerves from the mandibular nerve.

expert.summary: Lateral pterygoid has two heads and inserts on the condylar neck, articular disc and joint capsule of the TMJ.

points.text: The upper head arises from the greater wing of the sphenoid; the lower head from the lateral pterygoid plate.
It inserts on the pterygoid fovea of the condylar neck and on the disc and capsule of the temporomandibular joint.

checks.q: Which movement does the lateral pterygoid help with?
checks.explain: It assists with protrusion and side-to-side movement.

beginner.summary: The buccinator is a deep cheek muscle that keeps food from pooling in the cheek.

points.text: It tightens the cheek so food does not pocket there while chewing.
It is supplied by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

expert.summary: Buccinator is a deep cheek muscle innervated by CN VII on its superficial surface.

points.text: Because it lies deep, it receives its facial nerve supply on its superficial surface.

checks.q: What does the buccinator do while you chew?
checks.explain: It tightens the cheek to keep food from pocketing.

beginner.summary: The zygomaticus major is the main smiling muscle.

points.text: It pulls the corner of the mouth up and outward when you smile.
It is supplied by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

expert.summary: Zygomaticus major inserts on the modiolus and receives zygomatic and buccal branches of CN VII.

points.text: It inserts on the modiolus at the corner of the mouth, and surgeons use it as a landmark for the modiolus.
It is the muscle most often replaced in facial reanimation surgery.

checks.q: What happens when the zygomaticus major contracts?
options: The mouth corner moves up and out
checks.explain: It lifts the mouth corner upward and outward in a smile.

beginner.summary: This muscle lifts the upper lip.

points.text: Its job is to raise the upper lip.
It is supplied by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

expert.summary: Levator labii superioris belongs to the lip elevator group and is also called quadratus labii.

points.text: It lies between levator labii superioris alaeque nasi (medial) and levator anguli oris (lateral and deeper).

checks.q: Which nerve supplies the levator labii superioris?
checks.explain: Facial expression muscles like this one are supplied by the facial nerve.

beginner.summary: The nasalis is a small nose muscle used when you scrunch your nose.

points.text: When you snarl, it creates vertical 'bunny lines' on the sides of the nose.
It is supplied by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

expert.summary: Nasalis is grouped with depressor septi and dilator naris; overuse is linked to bunny-line wrinkles.

points.text: The nasal muscles include nasalis, depressor septi and dilator naris.

checks.q: Which nerve supplies the nasalis?
checks.explain: The source lists the facial nerve as its supply.

beginner.summary: The tongue is a muscular organ that helps with taste and moving food.

points.text: It has four intrinsic muscles that change its shape and four extrinsic muscles that attach it to nearby bones.
Taste comes in five categories: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) moves all its muscles except the palatoglossus.

expert.summary: Tongue muscles are split into intrinsic and extrinsic groups, with taste and sensation carried by CN VII, V, IX and X.

points.text: Taste from the front two-thirds travels in the chorda tympani (CN VII); general sensation travels in the lingual nerve (V).
The back third sends taste and sensation through the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

clinical.text: Damage here can include hypoglossal injury, which makes the tongue deviate toward the injured side.

checks.q: Which nerve moves most tongue muscles?
checks.explain: The hypoglossal nerve supplies all tongue muscles except the palatoglossus.

beginner.summary: The hyoglossus pulls the tongue back and flattens its sides.

points.text: It pulls the tongue backward and lowers its side edges.
It is one of the four extrinsic tongue muscles.
It is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

expert.summary: Hyoglossus is an extrinsic tongue muscle arising from the hyoid body and supplied by CN XII.

points.text: It arises from the lateral part of the anterior body of the hyoid bone.

checks.q: What does the hyoglossus do to the tongue?
checks.explain: It retracts the tongue and depresses its lateral margins.

beginner.summary: Skin covers the body and acts as its first barrier against the outside world.

points.text: It has three layers: epidermis, dermis, and the deeper hypodermis.
It protects against microbes, drying out, UV light and mechanical injury.
It also senses touch, pressure, pain and temperature and helps regulate temperature.

expert.summary: Skin comprises epidermis, dermis (papillary and reticular) and subcutaneous tissue, with keratinocytes, melanocytes, Langerhans and Merkel cells.

points.text: Melanocytes make pigment and Merkel cells act as tactile pressure receptors.
Skin is thickest on the palms and soles and thinnest on the eyelids.

clinical.text: Damage here can include skin cancers; the three most common are basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma.

checks.q: Which is the outermost layer of skin?
checks.explain: The epidermis is the outermost layer.

beginner.summary: The digastric has two bellies under the jaw and helps open the mouth and swallow.

points.text: It pulls the chin down and back to help open the mouth.
It also lifts the hyoid bone during swallowing.
The back belly is supplied by the facial nerve; the front belly by a branch of the mandibular nerve.

expert.summary: Digastric has anterior and posterior bellies joined by an intermediate tendon held to the hyoid by a fascial sling.

points.text: The posterior belly arises from the mastoid notch; the anterior belly from the digastric fossa of the mandible.
The posterior belly is a surgical landmark, as the hypoglossal, accessory and vagus nerves pass deep to it.

checks.q: How many bellies does the digastric have?
checks.explain: Digastric means two bellies, joined by a tendon.

beginner.summary: The stylohyoid pulls the hyoid bone up and back during swallowing.

points.text: It pulls the hyoid backward and upward.
This lifts the tongue and lengthens the floor of the mouth to help swallowing.
It is supplied by the facial nerve.

expert.summary: Stylohyoid arises from the styloid process and inserts on the hyoid at the junction of body and greater horn.

points.text: It arises from the middle of the styloid process and inserts on the hyoid above the omohyoid.

clinical.text: Damage here can include Eagle syndrome from partial ossification of the stylohyoid ligament, with throat pain or trouble swallowing.

checks.q: Which nerve supplies the stylohyoid?
checks.explain: The source lists the facial nerve.

beginner.summary: A strong neck muscle that runs from the breastbone and collarbone up to the skull behind the ear.

points.text: It starts at the top of the breastbone and the inner part of the collarbone.
It attaches to the mastoid process, the bony bump behind the ear.
Working on one side, it tilts the head toward that side and turns the face to the other side.

expert.summary: Two heads merge into one belly that inserts on the mastoid process and superior nuchal line, mainly supplied by cranial nerve XI.

points.text: It inserts on the mastoid process and the front part of the superior nuchal line of the skull.
Its motor supply is mainly the accessory nerve (CN XI); cervical plexus fibers carry proprioception.
Branches of the external carotid artery, including the occipital and superior thyroid arteries, supply it.

clinical.text: Damage here can weaken the muscle and cause torticollis, a head tilt, if the accessory nerve is injured.

checks.q: Which bony landmark does the sternocleidomastoid attach to on the skull?
checks.explain: The muscle inserts on the mastoid process of the temporal bone.

beginner.summary: A broad muscle of the upper back and neck that moves the shoulder blade and helps hold posture.

points.text: It begins on the skull base, the ligament at the back of the neck, and the spine from C7 to T12.
It attaches to the shoulder blade and the outer part of the collarbone.
It is mainly a posture muscle, and it also helps with shoulder and head movement.

expert.summary: Upper, middle and lower fibers have different actions on the scapula; motor supply comes from CN XI.

points.text: Upper fibers extend the head and neck and raise the scapula; middle fibers pull the scapulae together; lower fibers depress it.
Motor supply is the spinal accessory nerve; pain and proprioception travel in the ventral rami of C3 and C4.
The transverse cervical artery is most often the main blood source.

clinical.text: Damage here can weaken the trapezius if the spinal accessory nerve is injured.

checks.q: Which nerve controls the trapezius muscle?
checks.explain: Motor supply to the trapezius is the spinal accessory nerve.

beginner.summary: A deep side-neck muscle that links the neck vertebrae to the first rib.

points.text: It starts on the sides of the lower six neck vertebrae.
It attaches to the top of the first rib.
The scalene muscles help with deep breathing and with bending the neck sideways.

expert.summary: It attaches from C2-C7 transverse processes to rib 1 and, with the anterior scalene, bounds the gap that the brachial plexus passes through.

points.text: Origin is the transverse processes of the last six cervical vertebrae; insertion is the first rib behind the subclavian artery groove.
The anterior and middle scalenes bound the interscalene gap through which the brachial plexus passes.

clinical.text: A tight middle scalene may involve the suprascapular nerve, which can weaken the supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

checks.q: Where does the middle scalene insert?
checks.explain: It inserts on the upper surface of the first rib.

beginner.summary: A muscle in front of the neck vertebrae that bends the head forward.

points.text: It lies in front of the neck spine, roughly from C1 to C6.
It attaches to the base of the skull, on the occipital bone.
It flexes the head at the joint between skull and spine.

expert.summary: It arises from the C3-C6 anterior tubercles and transverse processes and inserts on the basilar occipital bone.

points.text: Origin is the anterior tubercles and transverse processes of C3 to C6; insertion is the basilar part of the occipital bone.
It receives branches from the ventromedial parts of the C1 to C3 ventral rami.

checks.q: What movement does the longus capitis perform?
checks.explain: It flexes the head at the craniocervical junction.

beginner.summary: A long, flat muscle on the front of the neck spine that helps bend the head forward.

points.text: It lies on the front surface of the spine.
It has three parts: superior oblique, inferior oblique, and vertical.
Both sides together flex the head; one side tilts it.

expert.summary: Its superior oblique part runs C3-C5 up to C1 and its inferior oblique part T1-T3 up to C5-C6, supplied by C2-C6 ventral rami.

points.text: Superior oblique part: C3-C5 up to C1. Inferior oblique part: T1-T3 up to C5 and C6.
Ventromedial branches of the C2 to C6 ventral rami supply it.

clinical.text: Damage here can include tendonitis, which can contribute to neck pain.

checks.q: Where is the longus colli located?
options: On the front of the spine
On the back of the skull
checks.explain: It lies on the anterior surface of the spine.

beginner.summary: A small muscle just under the skull that nods the head.

points.text: It lies in front of the upper neck spine, behind the prevertebral fascia.
It runs from the first neck vertebra (C1) to the skull base.
With both sides acting it flexes the head; one side bends the head sideways.

expert.summary: It runs from the C1 transverse process to the jugular process of the occipital bone, supplied by the anterior ramus of C1.

points.text: Origin is the transverse process of C1; insertion is the jugular process of the occipital bone.
The ascending pharyngeal artery supplies it.

checks.q: Which vertebra does the rectus capitis anterior start from?
checks.explain: It arises from the transverse process of C1.

topics.title: Rectus capitis posterior major and minor

beginner.summary: Two small suboccipital muscles at the back of the neck that extend the head.

points.text: Both attach to the lower ridge (inferior nuchal line) of the skull.
The major starts on the C2 spinous process; the minor starts on the back of C1.
They extend the neck and turn the head to the same side.

expert.summary: Both insert on the inferior nuchal line and, like all suboccipital muscles, are supplied by the suboccipital nerve (C1 dorsal ramus).

points.text: Major arises from the C2 spinous process; minor arises from the posterior tubercle of C1.
The suboccipital nerve, the dorsal ramus of C1, supplies all four suboccipital muscles.
Rectus capitis posterior major forms the superomedial border of the suboccipital triangle.

clinical.text: Damage here can occur as strain or spasm in whiplash-type injuries.

checks.q: Which nerve supplies the suboccipital muscles?
