checks.explain: All four suboccipital muscles are supplied by the suboccipital nerve.

beginner.summary: Two small muscles at the top of the neck, not related to the eye, that help turn and tilt the head.

points.text: The superior one runs from the side of C1 to the skull; the inferior one runs from C2 to C1.
The inferior oblique turns the head to the same side.
The superior oblique helps extend and bend the head sideways.

expert.summary: Obliquus capitis superior and inferior form the lateral borders of the suboccipital triangle, which holds the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve.

points.text: Superior arises from the C1 transverse process and inserts on the occipital bone between the nuchal lines.
Inferior arises from the C2 spinous process and inserts on the C1 transverse process.
The suboccipital triangle contains the suboccipital nerve, the third part of the vertebral artery, and a venous plexus.

checks.q: Which vertebra does the obliquus capitis inferior start from?
checks.explain: It arises from the spinous process of C2.

beginner.summary: A superficial back-of-neck muscle that turns and lifts the head.

points.text: It starts on the spine from C7 to the upper thoracic vertebrae.
It attaches to the mastoid process and the outer part of the superior nuchal line.
One side turns the head to the same side; both sides extend the head.

expert.summary: A splenius group muscle of the superficial back layer, supplied by lateral branches of the C2-C3 dorsal rami.

points.text: Origin is the spinous processes of C7 and T1-T3 (or T4) and the supraspinous ligaments.
Lateral branches of the C2-C3 dorsal rami supply it.

checks.q: What does the splenius capitis do when both sides contract?
checks.explain: Bilateral contraction extends the head.

beginner.summary: The top part of the erector spinae, a deep back muscle group, reaching the skull behind the ear.

points.text: It belongs to the erector spinae group of deep back muscles.
It starts on the transverse processes of C4 to T4.
It attaches to the back edge of the mastoid process.

expert.summary: It is the capitis part of the longissimus group of the erector spinae, running from C4-T4 transverse processes to the mastoid process.

points.text: The source states origin on C4-T4 transverse processes and insertion on the posterior mastoid process.
The same source says the actions of the cervical and capitis erector spinae parts are unknown.

checks.q: Which muscle group does the longissimus capitis belong to?
checks.explain: It is part of the longissimus group of the erector spinae.

beginner.summary: A posterior neck muscle that extends the head and bends or rotates it.

points.text: It is one of the posterior neck muscles in the transversospinalis group.
When both sides contract, they extend the head and neck.
One side bends the head to its own side and rotates it to the opposite side.

expert.summary: It forms the roof of the suboccipital triangle and, in the transversospinalis group, extends the head bilaterally.

points.text: Unilateral contraction gives ipsilateral lateral flexion and contralateral rotation.
It forms the roof of the suboccipital triangle.

checks.q: Which muscle forms the roof of the suboccipital triangle?
checks.explain: The suboccipital triangle roof is semispinalis capitis.

beginner.summary: A muscle that lifts the soft palate when you swallow.

points.text: It begins near the eustachian tube and temporal bone and attaches to the palate's tendon sheet.
It raises the soft palate, closing off the nasal part of the throat during swallowing.
Branches of the vagus nerve supply it.

expert.summary: It contributes about 40% of soft palate length and sets the alpha angle, linked to airway shape in sleep apnea.

points.text: It arises from the eustachian tube and petrous temporal bone and inserts into the palatine aponeurosis.
It makes up about 40% of the length of the soft palate.
Its supply is the pharyngeal plexus (vagus, CN X).

checks.q: What does the levator veli palatini do during swallowing?
checks.explain: It elevates the soft palate and closes off the nasopharynx.

beginner.summary: A muscle that tightens the soft palate when you swallow.

points.text: It starts at the medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone.
It tenses the soft palate, helping keep food out of the nose side of the throat.
It is the only palate muscle not supplied by the vagus nerve.

expert.summary: It runs from the medial pterygoid plate to the palatine aponeurosis, supplied by the trigeminal medial pterygoid nerve.

points.text: It arises at the medial pterygoid plate and attaches to the palatine aponeurosis.
The medial pterygoid nerve, a trigeminal branch, supplies it.

checks.q: Which palate muscle is NOT supplied by the vagus nerve?
checks.explain: The tensor veli palatini is supplied by a branch of the trigeminal nerve.

beginner.summary: A thin muscle linking the soft palate to the side of the tongue.

points.text: It starts at the palate's tendon sheet and ends in the side of the tongue.
It pulls the soft palate toward the tongue and helps start swallowing.
Two arches bind the soft palate to the tongue and pharynx, and the tonsils lie between them.

expert.summary: Arising from the palatine aponeurosis to the tongue side, it forms the palatoglossal arch and is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.

points.text: It runs down, forward and out from the palatine aponeurosis to the lateral tongue.
The pharyngeal plexus (vagus) supplies it.

checks.q: Which structure does the palatoglossus connect the soft palate to?
checks.explain: It inserts into the side of the tongue.

beginner.summary: A muscle running from the palate down the throat wall that helps with swallowing.

points.text: It begins at the hard palate and palatine aponeurosis and attaches to the thyroid cartilage.
It pulls the pharynx up and forward during swallowing and helps close the airway.
The vagus nerve supplies it.

expert.summary: Arising from the hard palate and aponeurosis to the thyroid cartilage's upper border, it is supplied via the pharyngeal plexus.

points.text: It inserts on the superior border of the thyroid cartilage.
The source describes its role as tensing the soft palate and closing the laryngeal airway; its introduction wording differs.

clinical.text: A distal palatal segment longer than 15 mm is linked to higher sleep apnea risk and poorer surgical outcomes.

checks.q: What does the palatopharyngeus help close during swallowing?
checks.explain: It closes the laryngeal airway to help prevent aspiration.

beginner.summary: The small dangling tip of the soft palate, moved by a small muscle.

points.text: Its muscle, the musculus uvulae, comes from the palate's tendon sheet and the posterior nasal spine.
It attaches to the lining of the uvula and shortens it.
The vagus nerve supplies it.

expert.summary: Musculus uvulae shortens the uvula, with one-sided contraction raising that side, supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.

points.text: It originates from the palatine aponeurosis and posterior nasal spine and inserts into uvular mucosa.
Ipsilateral contraction draws the uvula up on the same side.

clinical.text: UPPP, the most common surgery for obstructive sleep apnea, repositions or removes soft palate and uvula tissue.

checks.q: What does the musculus uvulae do?
checks.explain: It shortens the uvula.

beginner.summary: A throat muscle that squeezes food downward during swallowing.

points.text: It starts at the hyoid bone and the lower part of the stylohyoid ligament.
Its fibers meet at the pharyngeal raphe in the midline.
It pushes the swallowed bolus downward.

expert.summary: It arises from the hyoid cornua and stylohyoid ligament, inserts on the pharyngeal raphe, and is vagus-supplied.

points.text: Origin is the lower stylohyoid ligament and both hyoid cornua; insertion is the pharyngeal raphe.
The vagus nerve supplies all pharyngeal muscles except stylopharyngeus, so it supplies this muscle.

checks.q: What does the middle constrictor do during swallowing?
checks.explain: It propels the bolus downward.

beginner.summary: A slim throat muscle that lifts the pharynx and voice box during swallowing.

points.text: It starts at the styloid process, a bony spike below the ear.
It lifts the larynx and pharynx and widens the pharynx to move food.
It is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

expert.summary: The only pharyngeal muscle arising outside the pharyngeal wall and supplied by CN IX, it inserts mainly on the thyroid cartilage.

points.text: It is the only pharyngeal muscle originating outside the pharyngeal wall.
Some fibers join palatopharyngeus to insert on the posterior border of the thyroid lamina.
The pharyngeal branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery supplies it.

clinical.text: Damage here can follow bilateral glossopharyngeal nerve anesthesia, which can impair this muscle and collapse the nasopharyngeal back wall.

checks.q: Which nerve supplies the stylopharyngeus?
checks.explain: It is supplied by CN IX, unlike other pharyngeal muscles.

beginner.summary: The precuneus is a part of the inner parietal lobe that brain imaging links to space, memory and self.

points.text: Brain-imaging studies link the precuneus to visual-spatial perception, memory retrieval, self-related thinking and consciousness.
One paper calls it one of the brain's main centres of integration.
Its rear part sits just in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus; its front part sits just behind the cingulate sulcus's marginal branch.

expert.summary: Its parts connect to the cingulum and, through the splenium, to the opposite hemisphere.

points.text: The rear part (7m) has white-matter links to the cingulum; both parts link to the opposite hemisphere.
Within the parietal lobe it connects mostly to the intraparietal sulcus and angular gyrus.
Differences in its length are a major source of variation in adult midline brain shape.

checks.q: Which groove lies just behind the rear part of the precuneus?
checks.explain: The chapter places the rear precuneus just in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus.

beginner.summary: The intraparietal sulcus is a deep groove across the parietal lobe, and its front end begins at the postcentral sulcus.

points.text: The intraparietal sulcus is a deep groove that separates the superior parietal lobule from the inferior parietal lobule.
Its front end starts at the postcentral sulcus and its back end joins the parieto-occipital sulcus.
The front part of the sulcus is a well-established grasping region.

expert.summary: Along its length, different parts handle different steps of reaching and grasping.

points.text: It is about 4.5 cm long and in places deeper than 3 cm.
Middle part: turns what you see into motor programs for reaching, and is active in eye movements guided by vision.
Back part: is believed to help analyse object features such as texture and orientation for grasping.

clinical.text: Damage to the outer bank of the front part can impair how the hand shapes to grasp.

checks.q: Which part of the intraparietal sulcus is a well-established grasping region?
checks.explain: The review identifies the anterior (front) intraparietal sulcus as a well-established grasping region.

topics.title: White matter of the cerebral hemispheres

beginner.summary: White matter is the myelinated wiring under the cortex that lets brain regions talk to each other.

points.text: White matter lies beneath the cortex, the outer gray layer of the cerebrum.
Its axons are wrapped in myelin, which gives the tissue its white look.
This myelinated wiring lets different brain regions communicate quickly.

expert.summary: Oligodendrocytes make up most of its cells, and the corpus callosum links the two hemispheres.

points.text: Oligodendrocytes are the most prominent cell type in white matter.
The corpus callosum keeps the left and right hemispheres in contact.

clinical.text: Demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis can show up as plaques beside the ventricles on MRI.

checks.q: What gives white matter its pale color?
checks.explain: Myelinated axons look white; unmyelinated tissue looks gray.

beginner.summary: The lateral orbital gyrus is part of the lateral orbitofrontal cortex on the underside of the frontal lobe.

points.text: Brodmann's area 47 spans this gyrus and reaches into the nearby lower frontal cortex.
Two mapped areas, Fo6 and Fo7, lie in this region; Fo7 sits mainly in the lateral orbital sulcus and inner half of the gyrus.
The orbital surface commonly shows an H-shaped pattern of grooves.

expert.summary: Cell-structure mapping divides the region into areas such as Fo6 and Fo7, and groove patterns vary between people.

points.text: Fo6 occupies the gyrus and part of the lateral orbital sulcus; a branch of the horizontal fissure marks its border with area 46.
In 52 hemispheres, the authors found four types of orbital groove pattern, with H-shaped the most common on the left.

checks.q: Which Brodmann area spans the lateral orbital gyrus?
checks.explain: The study says area 47 spans this gyrus and extends into nearby lower frontal cortex.

beginner.summary: The collateral sulcus is a groove on the underside of the temporal lobe beside the parahippocampal gyrus.

points.text: It forms the lateral border of the parahippocampal gyrus on the temporal lobe's underside.
Its lateral border forms the lateral edge of the parahippocampal gyrus.
Its medial bank is the perirhinal cortex.

expert.summary: Different parts of the sulcus mark the borders of the perirhinal cortex.

points.text: The top of the sulcus marks the outer edge of the perirhinal cortex.
Its lower part marks the border between perirhinal and entorhinal cortex.

checks.q: Which gyrus has its lateral edge formed by the collateral sulcus?
checks.explain: The review says the sulcus's lateral border forms the lateral edge of the parahippocampal gyrus.

beginner.summary: The ambiens gyrus is a bump on the inner side of the front temporal lobe, mostly entorhinal cortex.

points.text: It is a prominence on the medial side of the anterior medial temporal lobe.
The authors describe it as a medial extension of the parahippocampal gyrus.
A groove called the sulcus semianularis bounds it above, and the intrarhinal sulcus bounds it below.

expert.summary: Its cortex matches an entorhinal subfield, so Brodmann area 34 is treated as part of entorhinal cortex.

points.text: It is largely formed by the medial intermediate entorhinal subfield (EMI), and its cortex is periallocortex.
Older work assigned it to the olfactory system; the authors instead group it with entorhinal cortex (area 28).

checks.q: The ambiens gyrus is described as an extension of which gyrus?
checks.explain: The authors describe it as a medial extension of the parahippocampal gyrus.

steps.predict: Before we start: how many major regions do you think the brain is divided into?
steps.text: Anatomists describe four major regions: cerebrum, diencephalon, brain stem, and cerebellum. This tour visits each one.
From above you see the cerebrum's two hemispheres, separated by the longitudinal fissure. The wrinkled surface is the cerebral cortex.

steps.predict: The two hemispheres need to talk. Where do you think the bridge between them is?
steps.text: Deep in the middle, the corpus callosum carries most of the traffic between the hemispheres.
The frontal lobe: movement, planning, and much of what we call personality.
The central sulcus divides frontal from parietal. In front of it, the precentral gyrus moves the body; behind it, the postcentral gyrus feels the body.
The temporal lobe, below the lateral sulcus: hearing and memory.
The occipital lobe at the back is where vision first reaches the cortex.
The diencephalon sits at the center. The thalamus relays almost all senses to the cortex; the hypothalamus keeps the body in balance.

steps.predict: Which region do you think keeps you breathing without thinking about it?
steps.text: The brain stem: midbrain, pons, and medulla. The medulla regulates breathing and heart function.
The cerebellum compares intended movement with what actually happened and corrects it. You now know the four regions; try the Quiz to lock them in.
Commands start in the primary motor cortex, whose upper motor neurons instruct the spinal cord.

steps.predict: Which deep structures do you think decide whether a movement is allowed to start?
steps.text: The basal nuclei gate movement. Cortical input enters the striatum (caudate and putamen).
Dopamine from the substantia nigra activates the direct pathway and inhibits the indirect pathway.
Basal nuclei output returns to the cortex through the thalamus.
Copies of motor commands travel through the pons to the cerebellum.
The cerebellum compares the command with sensory feedback (via the inferior olive) and sends corrections to the midbrain.

steps.predict: Where do you think new long-term memories are formed? Look at the inside of the temporal lobe.
steps.text: The hippocampus, deep in the temporal lobe, is central to forming lasting memories.
Its main output is the fornix, an arching bundle heading toward the anterior thalamus and hypothalamus.
Just in front of the hippocampus, the amygdala processes fear and adds emotional weight to memories.
The amygdala reaches the hypothalamus, which drives the body's autonomic and hormonal responses.

tours.title: From eye to sight: the visual pathway

steps.predict: Where in the brain do you think seeing happens: just behind the eyes, or somewhere else?
steps.text: Light is detected in the retina at the back of each eye, but seeing happens much farther back, in the visual cortex of the occipital lobe. This tour follows the signal there.
Each retina sends its signals out of the eye along an optic nerve.

steps.predict: Does each eye report only to its own side of the brain?
steps.text: The two optic nerves meet at the optic chiasm. Fibres from the nose-side half of each retina cross to the other side here; fibres from the outer half stay on their own side.

Behind the chiasm the fibres continue as the optic tracts. Because of the partial crossing, each side of the brain now carries the opposite half of what you see: the left side handles the right half of your view.
Most optic tract fibres end in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, the relay station on the way to the cortex.
Some fibres go to the superior colliculus in the midbrain instead. It combines sight, sound and touch and helps turn the head toward something that grabs your attention.

steps.predict: If something is at the top of your view, do you think the top or the bottom of the visual cortex handles it?
steps.text: Neurons in the lateral geniculate nucleus send their axons to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe, mostly on its inner wall along the calcarine sulcus. The map is flipped: the upper part of the visual cortex handles the lower part of your view.

From the visual cortex, information flows along two streams. A lower stream into the temporal lobe works out what you are looking at; an upper stream into the parietal lobe works out where it is and guides your movements.

tours.title: How a sound reaches the cortex

steps.predict: A sound arrives at your right ear a split second before your left. What could the brain use that for?
steps.text: Signals from the inner ear enter the brain stem at the cochlear nuclei, in the upper medulla. Brain stem nuclei then combine input from both ears and use the small differences in timing and loudness to work out where a sound came from.
Auditory signals continue up to the inferior colliculus in the midbrain.
One branch goes to the superior colliculus, which helps turn your head and neck toward the sound.
The main branch goes to the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, the relay for hearing.
The medial geniculate nucleus passes the signal to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe, where sound is consciously heard.

steps.predict: If you touch something with your left hand, which side of the brain do you think feels it?
steps.text: Fine touch and body-position signals climb the back of the spinal cord in the dorsal column system and reach two nuclei in the medulla, the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus. The next neuron's axon crosses the midline here, so touch on the left side of the body is handled by the right side of the brain.
After crossing, the axons rise through the brain stem as a bundle called the medial lemniscus and end in the thalamus, where they connect with the third neuron of the pathway.
The third neuron projects to the postcentral gyrus, where the touch is first processed by the cortex and becomes a conscious sensation.

steps.predict: Do you think your back or your fingertips get more cortex?
steps.text: The postcentral gyrus holds a map of the body, but not a scale model: sensitive areas such as the fingers and lower face take up far more cortex than the shoulders and back.
Pain and temperature take a different route, the spinothalamic tract, which crosses in the spinal cord at the level where the signal enters instead of in the medulla.
